newsitem.title: USA: Brokers differ on COMEX copper strip trade move.
newsitem.headline: Brokers differ on COMEX copper strip trade move.

text.p: Brokers hold mixed views on strip trading in COMEX copper futures, the New York exchange's latest move to win back market share from its LME rival across the Atlantic.

A spokeswoman for NYMEX, of which COMEX is a division, said there was a great deal of interest among the commercials on the exchange in strip trading which, currently only available over-the-counter (OTC).
"This gives you the best of both worlds - the efficiency of a single transaction and the liquidity and integrity of an exchange traded product," the spokeswoman said.
From Sept 20, brokers will be able to buy or sell copper futures contracts from two to 24 consecutive months for an average price traded in one single execution.
The average price would be calculated by the broker. A margin would be payable on each contract traded.
A minimum of one contract would have to be traded in each of the months in the calendar strip, but once the deal is executed, any contracts may be delivered or liquidated.
"This would allow you to do long-term planning at a fixed rate as opposed to right now hedging individually at varied expenses," the NYMEX spokeswoman said.
Average pricing has been standard fare on LME copper for a long time.

"You could not do this on COMEX, so you had to sell whatever lots in every month and trading the odd months, that is, the non-active months, was a nightmare," an LME ring dealing broker said. "It certainly detracted from business and by having the ability to quote the strip as an average price, it should enhance business."

Another broker argued that allowing strip trading is one thing, "but to have people there who will make markets and take the other side is something quite different. To change the way COMEX trades, you have to change the people who trade on it."
The ring dealer countered: "People will step up to the plate."

Broker Craig Dubitsky of Smith Barney said COMEX's move was a good attempt but would probably be "rough going" at the start because average pricing "is such a foreign element for most of the people" on COMEX.

"I don't know if the liquidity will be there or if people will take the time to sit there and do average pricing on a one-off basis," Dubitsky said. "Eventually it will work because it's the norm for the rest of the world."

Meanwhile, COMEX is set to fell stiffer competition from the LME from January 1997 when the London exchange is due to introduce its Trade Average Price Options - TAPOs - which are an exchange cleared type of options contract for copper and primary aluminum, currently traded OTC as Asian options.
"The introduction of this trading vehicle is a reflection of the increased use by industry of average pricing for physical contracts," the exchange said in its Ringsider newsletter.
